<reason>Side B (PRO) won the decisive clash. CON's burden-shifting move — demanding a transaction that is fully informed, competent, voluntary, and harm-free yet unethical — backfired, because PRO correctly showed that those very conditions are extra things beyond the bare "yes," which is exactly what "consent alone is not enough" claims ([B2.1]-[B2.2], crystallized in [B5.1]-[B5.2]). CON's only answer was the assertion that information, competence, and voluntariness "are what consent is" ([A5.1]-[A5.2]), a semantic counter that never fully neutralized the charge of definitional gerrymandering given the motion's plain wording. PRO's gambler test case survived pressure: the "every sale exploits psychology" dilemma ([A3.1]) was met with a workable line between delivering wanted value and profiting from engineered error ([B4.1]-[B4.2]), and the "name the wronged party" pressure ([A3.2]) was answered honestly with the manipulation-wrong and the "lying to a friend needs no lawsuit" analogy ([B4.3]). CON's third-party-harm "separate wrong" analysis was its strongest surviving ground, and PRO's structural-dependence reply kept it contested rather than settled. CON was rhetorically sharper and executed the A1/A2 format cleanly, but three clipped speeches and a burden that arguably conceded PRO's thesis cost it. PRO gave the cleaner reason to vote and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]-[B2.2]) exposing CON's "fully consensual" demand as smuggling in fairness and adequate alternatives — restating PRO's thesis as a refutation — was the decisive exchange, and CON's "that's what consent IS" reply in closing never fully recovered from it.</best_rebuttal>
